did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens by addressing sons in the plural and presenting the father’s teaching as instruction they should heed in order to gain understanding.
Did you know? The speaker describes himself as a tender, only child in his father’s and mother’s presence, presenting wisdom as a tradition passed down from one generation to the next.
Did you know? The command “Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding” emphasizes that wisdom and understanding require pursuit and effort, not merely passive acceptance.
Did you know? Wisdom is described in feminine terms and almost as a person: she must not be forsaken, she should be loved, and she will protect and guard a person.
Did you know? According to the chapter, wisdom is more than intellectual knowledge: when she is exalted and embraced, she bestows honor and protects a person with a crown of glory.
Did you know? The way of wisdom is described as a path that allows a person to walk and run without stumbling—in other words, a steady and secure way to live.
Did you know? The warning against the way of the wicked is presented in stages: do not enter their path, do not walk in the way of evil people; turn away from it and move on.

Did you know? The wicked are described through images of eating and drinking: they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence. These images emphasize how deeply evil has become their habit.

Did you know? The chapter draws a central contrast between the ways of the righteous and the wicked: the path of the righteous grows brighter until full daylight, while the way of the wicked is like deep darkness, and they do not know what will make them stumble.
Did you know? The command “Guard your heart above all else” is explained by the fact that the sources of life flow from it, placing the heart at the center of the chapter’s moral instruction.
